primary_claim: In ResNet-18 models trained on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, an active-learning (least-confidence uncertainty sampling) training regime does not reduce superposition relative to a standard baseline -- it instead shows more superposition (higher mean cosine similarity, lower silhouette score, more class-cluster overlap) than the baseline, contrary to the hypothesis that focusing training on uncertain/difficult samples would reduce superposition.

effect.metric: mean cosine similarity between neuron representations / silhouette score (active learning vs baseline)
effect.value: CIFAR-10: cosine sim AL 0.927 vs baseline 0.885; silhouette AL 0.189 vs baseline 0.212

stated_future_work: examine different data sampling strategies from the Active Learning methods to see if there is a difference in the Superposition based on them
Working with a deeper model and a better quality dataset to conduct the same experiment
limitations_stated: due to the lack of computational resources, the smaller vision datasets CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet were used
As the CIFAR-10 image data size is very small, it is hard to interpret what features the neurons are exactly activating for
these units are not reacting to the same features as they are from different models... so we can not directly compare them
quote: Contrary to my expectations, the active learning model did not significantly outperform the baseline in terms of feature separation and overall accuracy.
